content: Low birth weight and premature infants are at a significantly increased risk of developing severe hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice, which can progress to bilirubin encephalopathy. Phototherapy is the most commonly used treatment for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and may be most effective in preventing the complications of hyperbilirubinemia when initiated as a prophylactic measure. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of prophylactic phototherapy in preterm infants (gestational age less than 37 weeks) or those with low birth weight (less than 2500 grams). The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, up to March 31, 2011. They included randomized controlled trials or quasi-randomized controlled studies that evaluated the effects of prophylactic phototherapy in this population. Two independent authors extracted data from the included studies. A fixed-effect meta-analysis was performed to evaluate outcomes such as the rate of exchange transfusion, the incidence of cerebral palsy or other neurodevelopmental impairments, peak serum bilirubin levels, and all-cause mortality. A total of nine studies involving 3449 participants were included in the analysis. One study with liberal transfusion criteria demonstrated a significant reduction in the rate of exchange transfusion with prophylactic phototherapy (risk ratio [RR] 0.20; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.13 to 0.31). However, two more recent studies with stricter transfusion criteria did not show a statistically significant reduction in exchange transfusion rates (typical RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.19 to 2.28). There was no statistically significant difference in the incidence of cerebral palsy between the prophylactic phototherapy group and the control group (typical RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.50 to 1.85; two studies, 756 participants). However, one large study that assessed neurodevelopmental impairment as a composite outcome (including cerebral palsy) found a slightly lower rate of neurodevelopmental impairment in the prophylactic phototherapy group (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.74 to 0.99; 1804 participants). Prophylactic phototherapy was associated with lower peak serum bilirubin levels (mean difference [MD] -2.73 mg/dL; 95% CI -2.89 to -2.57; six studies, 2319 participants). Additionally, fewer neonates in the prophylactic phototherapy group had peak unconjugated serum bilirubin levels exceeding 10 mg/dL (typical RR 0.27; 95% CI 0.22 to 0.33; three studies, 1090 participants) or 15 mg/dL (typical RR 0.13; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.23; four studies, 1116 participants). There was no statistically significant difference in all-cause mortality between the prophylactic phototherapy group and the control group (typical RR 1.08; 95% CI 0.93 to 1.26; four studies, 3044 participants). In conclusion, prophylactic phototherapy effectively reduces serum bilirubin levels and may influence the rates of exchange transfusion and neurodevelopmental impairment. However, further well-designed studies are necessary to evaluate its long-term efficacy and safety, particularly with respect to neurodevelopmental outcomes.
